newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures survived their initial jitters after the U.S. non-farm payrolls release, taking their cue from the Treasury market, to settle at the day's high.
A combination of short covering, relief that the jobs rise was not as bad as some had feared, a late franc rally and a positive response to French tax cut plans buoyed the market.
The franc rally, which pushed the currency to its highest level against the mark since August 26, also left PIBOR contracts at their day's highs.
The Treasury bumped up its OAT sales for the week to 20.1 billion, above the 16-18 billion it had planned to sell.

A foreign exchange trader said the franc had benefited from continued large sales of marks for francs by a non-resident corporate while concerns about Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health left investors reluctant to hold marks over the weekend.
The franc was trading at 3.4155 per mark at 1500 GMT, near the day's high of 3.4146, nearly a centime above the session low of 3.4240. It was last higher at 3.4138 on August 26.

Traders also said a general sentiment that the French and German central banks were resolved to defend the franc's old exchange rate mechanism floor of 3.4305 and the fact the tax cut announcement passed without incident helped to flush out shorts.

Eric Muller, economist at UBS in Paris said the principle of tax cutting was well received by the market on the grounds the economy needed some help. "The government has understood it needs to give it some oxygen," he said.

He said although the market still wanted to see the spending side of the budget, the fact the net size of tax cuts was relatively small calmed concerns they would significantly damage attempts to get the 1997 deficit down to three percent of GDP.
The progress of PIBOR contracts during the past two sessions demonstrated the fact that many who had taken aggressive positions against France had cut their positions, Muller said.

Tony Bolton at London Bond Broking said the surprise drop in the U.S. unemployment rate to 5.1 percent was mitigated to a certain extent because the actual rise in payrolls was broadly in line with expectations, helping bond markets to climb.

"They've already discounted a lot and there are people with an embarrassing amount of cash who are short of U.S. bonds, particularly in the five-year area," said Bolton. "There are not many sellers around."
The franc-driven boost to the short end in France steepened the curve slightly. The gap between two and 10-year bonds widened to 197 basis points from 195 on Thursday.
The two-year yield spread over German bonds narrowed four basis points while the 10-year yield spread came in one basis point.
